newsitem.title: USA: Israel envoy says PLO blocked dawn pact on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel envoy says PLO blocked dawn pact on Hebron.

text.p: Israel was expecting a dawn meeting with the Palestinians on Monday to conclude a deal on the West Bank town of Hebron but the Palestinians backtracked at the last minute, Israel's ambassador to Washington said.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat turned down an appeal from U.S. mediator Dennis Ross to postpone a trip to Europe later in the day, ruling out immediate prospects of an agreement, envoy Eliahu Ben Elissar said.

"Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu was ready and thought that he would be meeting with Yasser Arafat at Erez (on the Israel-Gaza border) somewhere around five o'clock," Ben Elissar told a news conference.
"Everything was ready for such a meeting in order to finalise an agreement," he said. "And then during the night the Palestinian side has reopened some of the paragraphs that had been agreed upon."

Ross later announced that he was returning to Washington after the two sides failed to clinch a deal on a partial Israeli withdrawal from Hebron. Arafat flew to Norway where he denied that he was stalling on an accord.

Ben Elissar said Ross had asked Arafat to postpone his trip, saying a Hebron agreement was more important. "But Yasser Arafat decided nevertheless to go to Europe without finalising the agreement," the envoy said.

Under agreements with the Palestinians, Israel was meant to redeploy its forces last spring in Hebron, where some 450 Jewish settlers live among more than 100,000 Arabs, but the move was delayed after Arab guerrilla attacks in Israel.

Ben Elissar said agreement had been reached with the Palestinians on "almost everything," although details on an Israeli right of hot pursuit into PLO-controlled areas after any guerrilla attack had been left for Netanyahu and Arafat.

One of the points reopened by the Palestinians concerned the arms to be used by Palestinian police, Ben Elissar said. The two sides had been close to agreement that the police would carry pistols and that rifles would be held in storage, to be used only by consent of both sides, he said.

He charged that statements by French President Jacques Chirac and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov had made Arafat more obdurate, although he stopped short of blaming them for the latest breakdown. "I blame Arafat," he said.
Chirac called last week for a Palestinian state and Primakov, who began a Middle East tour on Monday, has accused Israel in the past of stalling on the peace process.
"There is no doubt that Chirac's and Primakov's declarations made Dennis Ross's role more difficult," the Israeli ambassador said.

Some Israeli officials have suggested that Arafat is delaying the Hebron talks until after the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential election in the hope that a re-elected President Bill Clinton would press Israel to make concessions. But Ben Elissar said there was no prospect such a tactic would work. "They won't get from us more than what they got," he said.

Turning to Syria, Ben Elissar said Israeli concerns over Syrian troop movements had abated partly but not entirely following Syrian assurances through the United States that this was a routine autumn manoeuvre.
"We do not feel as much tension as we did feel a few days ago, but I can't say today that we are completely relieved. We are not," he said.
Israeli security sources said on Monday that defence chiefs had told Netanyahu the army needed more than $1 billion because of an increased chance of war with Syria.
